A low-carbohydrate intake does not improve high-intensity performance; instead, it reduces glycogen stores and increases reliance on fat oxidation, which is insufficient for high-intensity efforts. The claim that muscles compensate by increasing glycogen breakdown to improve performance is incorrect, since low carbohydrate intake limits glycogen availability. Thus, low carbohydrate intake results in greater reliance on muscle glycogen during exercise, which can impair high-intensity performance.

CONFIDENCE: 85
